Brief hides signatures, tasks, choosing and detail

Return Cow<str> when most inputs come back unchanged and only some need a new string.

Use it when
The common path can borrow, and callers mostly read the result.
Main drawback
The type and its lifetime spread into every signature that holds the result.
Simpler first
Return String until the extra allocation matters.
alloc · re-exported by stdadvice
At a glance
Defined in
alloc::borrow, re-exported as std::borrow
Stable since
Rust 1.0
Allocates
Not when borrowed. to_mut and into_owned make an owned copy of a borrowed value.
Bounds
B: ToOwned + ?Sized
Crates
None
linked source
Key signatures
Signature (simplified)What it does
to_mut(&mut self) -> &mut OwnedGives mutable access, cloning first if borrowed
into_owned(self) -> OwnedTakes the owned value, cloning if borrowed
deref(&self) -> &BLets you call the borrowed type's methods directly
Common tasks
Change it, cloning only if needed
Keep an owned value
Store a literal or a built string
Choosing
Return typeFits whenCosts
StringThe value is usually changed or must outlive the inputA new buffer when the output is non-empty
&strThe result is always part of the inputCannot return new text
Cow<str>Both happen, borrowing most oftenA lifetime and one more type to handle

What would change the choice: storing the result in a long-lived struct pushes towards String.

advice
Watch out
  • Calling into_owned() straight away gives up the saving.
  • A borrowed result keeps the input borrowed, so the input cannot be changed while it lives.
advice
More detail
Cost

The borrowed branch makes no new string. This page has no timing measurement yet. advice

When it fails

E0505: the input is moved while the borrowed result is still used.

Real code

String::from_utf8_lossy in the standard library returns Cow<str>: it borrows valid UTF-8 and allocates only to replace invalid bytes. linked source

See also
Cow
official docs

Every method and trait implementation.

from_utf8_lossy
std API

A real signature that returns a Cow.

A shared borrow is still in use when you try to change the same value.

Ways out: finish using first before the push, or copy the value out when it is cheap to copy.

DATABASES · EXECUTION

Join algorithms

Nested loop, sort-merge and hash joins: what each costs and when it wins.

5sections
337lines you can run
3 / 3tests passed, recorded
7further resources
Where it sits
  1. parser
  2. binder·planner
  3. optimizer
  4. executor
  5. access methods
  6. buffer pool
  7. disk
  8. transactions
  9. recovery
  10. distributed
IN 60 SECONDS
  • Joins exist because of normalization. Tables are decomposed to avoid redundancy, and joins reconstruct them. The focus is inner equijoins on two tables; everything else is a variation. Put the smaller table on the outer (left) side.
  • Output early materialization (copy values into new tuples; later operators never go back to the base tables; good for row stores) vs late materialization (copy only keys and record ids; good for column stores). Real systems mix both.
  • Cost model disk I/Os, ignoring output cost (the same for every algorithm). R has M pages and m tuples; S has N pages and n tuples.
  • Naive NLJ M + m·N. Block NLJ: M + M·N, and with B buffers (B−2 for the outer, 1 for the inner, 1 for output) M + ⌈M/(B−2)⌉·N. Index NLJ: M + m·C (C = cost per index probe; use an existing index or build a temporary one).
  • Sort-merge join sort both inputs (external sort costs), then merge with two cursors: M + N, degrading to M·N if every tuple has the same key. Best when inputs are already sorted (clustered index) or the output must be sorted.
  • Hash join equijoins on the full key only. Build a table on the outer side with h₁, then probe it with the inner side, re-checking the keys to handle collisions. Only the build side must fit in memory. A Bloom filter built alongside lets the probe side skip non-matches early (sideways information passing).
  • Grace hash join partition both inputs with h₁ to disk, then join partition pairs in memory. Re-partition with h₂ if a partition is too big, and use block NLJ for a single hot key that can't be split. Cost 3(M + N). Hybrid hash join keeps the hot partition in memory; it's rarely done in practice.
  • Rule of thumb hash is almost always best; sort-merge wins for skewed data, pre-sorted inputs, or sorted output. Good systems implement both.
01

Costs, reproduced

In memory, with no I/O at all, the picture changes:

Sort-merge is competitive with hash join in memory at this size because sort_unstable on 140k integers is extremely fast. Hash join wins as the build side outgrows cache or when the probe side is much larger (the build is O(m), and each probe is O(1)). NLJ loses by 40× even at a quarter of the input. The asymptotics are the lesson.

Watch out
NULL semantics in joins

NULL = NULL is UNKNOWN, so NULL keys never match in an inner join. Every algorithm above filters them out before building or partitioning, because a hash table that treats None == None as equal produces spurious matches. For outer joins, NULL-keyed outer rows appear unmatched. For anti joins, NOT EXISTS and NOT IN differ: NOT EXISTS keeps NULL-keyed outer rows, while NOT IN (subquery) returns nothing if the subquery yields any NULL (L02). The planner must implement NOT IN as a null-aware anti join.

In Rust
Returning pairs, not tuples

The reference joins return (left_id, right_id) pairs. That's late materialization: the caller fetches only the columns it needs. In the executor (P3), the same algorithms work on Tuples, and the output schema is left columns ++ right columns, so an early-materialized join copies both sides into a new Tuple. With Arrow-style batches (Part II), the join emits two index vectors, and a take kernel gathers the columns.

02

Run it

Reference: every join from the lecture, plus outer, semi and anti joins.

03

Choosing a join

Situation Best algorithm
Equijoin, build side fits in memory in-memory hash join (build on the smaller side)
Equijoin, both sides large Grace / partitioned hash join; radix-partitioned in memory (Part II)
Inputs already sorted on the key (clustered index, previous merge join) sort-merge, with no sort needed
Outer side tiny, inner side has an index on the key index nested loop
Non-equality predicate (a.x < b.y, band joins, LIKE) block NLJ (or sort-based band join)
Severe skew on one key hash join with a skew-aware partition, or sort-merge
Cyclic multi-way joins (graph patterns, triangles) worst-case optimal joins (Part II)
In production
In production
  • PostgreSQL: nested loop, merge join, and hash join (hybrid-style batching; parallel hash join since v11, with a shared hash table).
  • DuckDB, Velox, Umbra: radix-partitioned parallel hash joins, spilling per partition, with runtime join filters (min/max, and Bloom where it pays).
  • MySQL: nested loops only until 8.0.18 added hash join, a good illustration of how long a system can live without one.
04

Grace hash join, step by step

When neither side fits in memory, split both with the same hash and join them pair by pair.1Added for this mockup from the guide's Key ideas, to show the step-through block.

COMPILERS · TIPS AND TRICKS

Rust techniques

Patterns from rustc, swc and oxc, scaled down to Lox. The tags show which project each one comes from.

4sections
15tips
4code snippets
01

Lexer

Tip

Cursor over Chars, offset from what's left

Your offset() is already this pattern. Chars is just two pointers, so cloning it to peek costs almost nothing. rustc_lexer's Cursor uses first() and second() for the same job.

Seen inoxcrustc_lexer
Tip

Numbers need two characters of lookahead

In Lox, 12. lexes as Number Dot. Only eat the dot when peek2() is a digit. The slice-1 lexer tests check this.

Tip

The lexer never fails

rustc_lexer has no error type. An unknown character becomes an Unknown token, and a string literal has a terminated: bool flag. The next layer turns these into diagnostics. For Lox, emit Unknown or an unterminated String token and let the parser report it. That gives you a single error path.

Seen inrustc_lexer
Tip

Tokens carry spans, not values

rustc_lexer tokens store only a kind and a length. oxc reads identifier and literal text back from the source using the span. Parse the number in the parser with src[span].parse::<f64>(). The token then becomes Copy and 12 bytes.

Seen inrustc_lexeroxc
Tip

Compute line numbers when you need them

Don't count lines in the hot loop. Build a table of line starts once, and search it with a binary search when you report an error.

Seen inrustc SourceMap
Tip

Assert the sizes of hot types

rustc uses static_assert_size! on its AST and type nodes, and oxc asserts on its AST node sizes. A const assert like the last line above breaks the build when a new variant makes Token, Expr or Value bigger without you noticing.

Seen inrustcoxc
02

Parser

Tip

Use at, eat, expect and bump

Both parsers are built on this small set of helpers. The parser holds the current token and the end of the previous one, which lets you build a node's span from its first and last tokens.

Seen inrustcoxc
Tip

Pratt parsing for binary operators

The book writes one function per precedence level. A binding-power table replaces the equality, comparison, term and factor functions with one loop. Adding an operator is then one row in the table. Keep assignment and unary as ordinary functions.

Seen inmatklad
Tip

Recover, then keep going

rustc recovers from most syntax errors so it can report more than one per build. For Lox, the book's synchronize() is enough. Catch ParseError at the declaration level, skip to a statement boundary, and return all diagnostics at the end.

Seen inrustcmatklad
03

AST

Tip

Box is enough. Arenas are the upgrade

oxc allocates its whole AST in a bump arena (oxc_allocator::Box<'a, T>), and rustc uses typed arenas for its later IRs. For a Lox tree-walker, Box<Expr> is fast enough and simpler. If you try an arena, use Vec<Expr> with ExprId(u32) indices. The IDs then double as resolver keys.

Seen inoxcrustc
Tip

Use match instead of the Visitor pattern

Java needs visitors because it has no sum types. In Rust, each pass is a function that matches on the enum, and the compiler checks that every case is handled. rustc's Visitor trait and swc's generated Visit, VisitMut and Fold exist to walk hundreds of node types. Lox has about 20.

Seen inrustcswc
Tip

Identifiers: Rc<str> now, interning later

All three projects intern identifiers, so comparing two names is an integer compare and cloning one is free. Start with Rc<str>. If profiling shows HashMap<Rc<str>, _> hashing is slow, switch to a Symbol(u32) interner. matklad's interner post is about 40 lines, and the lasso crate is the ready-made version.

Seen inrustc Symbolswc Atomoxc Atom
04

Interpreter and errors

Tip

Write output to an injected writer

Pass &mut dyn Write to the interpreter. Tests pass a Vec<u8>, the CLI passes locked stdout, and fuzzing can pass io::sink().

Tip

thiserror in the library, anyhow only in main

Tests need to match on error kinds, so give the library a typed LoxError with Compile(Vec<Diagnostic>) and Runtime(RuntimeError). Its Display should print jlox's exact text, because the golden tests compare against it.

Tip

Pretty errors behind a flag

Your tokens already have spans, so rendering a source excerpt with a caret takes very little work. Use ariadne or miette in the REPL or behind --pretty. Keep the plain jlox format as the default so the official tests still pass.

Seen inoxc → miette

From “Lox in Rust, Slice by Slice”. Text is reused as written; the runnable files are formatted with rustfmt, other snippets are as written. Snippets: compiled and tested (confirmed by you). Claims and measurements: not checked here.

GUIDES · BY SYSTEM AND BY METHOD

Testing and benchmarking

How to know your code is correct, and how fast it is. Start from what you are building, or from a method.

12testing methods
3kinds of system
92planned pages
12resources shown here
01

Start from what you are testing

You are testingWhat says it is rightHow to find bugsShow the test can failWhat to benchmark
A distributed systemSafety and liveness checks; a linearizability checkerDeterministic simulation with fault injection; Jepsen-style testsInject a protocol bug and require a seed that catches itTail latency, throughput under load, recovery time
A databaseA reference model; logic-bug oracles; recovery invariantssqllogictest, differential queries, crash at every writeBreak an optimiser rule or skip a flushStandard workloads, read and write amplification
A compilerAn interpreter or another build as reference; an IR verifierGolden and compile-fail tests, fuzzing, random programs, reductionPlant a miscompile in one passCompile time, run time, code size
A service or APIThe contract: status, body, side effectsHandler tests, loopback tests, contract and schema-driven testsRemove an authorisation check and expect a failureLatency percentiles under load, saturation point
Async codeState after cancel, timeout and shutdownPaused time, cancellation at each await, stuck-task inspectionDrop a future mid-operation in a broken versionTask wake-ups, queue depth, tail latency
Concurrent or lock-free codeLinearizability; invariants after every steploom or shuttle, stress runs, ThreadSanitizerWeaken one atomic ordering and see which tool noticesScaling by thread count, contention, false sharing
Unsafe codeNo undefined behaviour from any safe use of the APIMiri, sanitizers, fuzzing the safe wrapper, bounded model checkingBreak a safety invariant in a copyThe unsafe version against the safe one it replaces

03

When each kind of test runs

When it runsWhat goes hereKeep it
While editingUnit and property tests for the code in handSeconds
Every pull requestAll fast tests, integration tests, lints, dependency advisoriesShort enough that people wait for it
NightlyLonger fuzzing, simulation seeds, Miri, sanitizers, mutation testsReproducible: record seeds and versions
Before a releaseSmoke tests on the built artifact, load and soak tests, benchmark comparisonCompared with the last release on the same machine
04

Tests that can fail

Watch out

A passing test can test nothing

While repairing the source cookbook, one loop-optimiser test never ran a program that traps, although it was meant to check traps. A pass told us nothing.

Testing

Prove the check can fail

For every important check, break the behaviour on purpose and require the check to fail. Keep that broken variant runnable, or let a mutation tool generate it.

Tip

Agreement is not correctness

A convergence check cannot see a bug that makes every replica wrong in the same way. Pair it with an independent oracle.

STANDARD LIBRARY AND CORE · API

HashMap's Entry API

map.entry(key) finds the key's place once and hands it to you as Occupied or Vacant, so you can read, insert, update or remove without looking it up again.

6sections
453lines you can run
12tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
IN 60 SECONDS
  • Use entry when what you do next depends on whether the key is there, and you may insert.
  • Counting is *map.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1; grouping is map.entry(k).or_default().push(v).
  • Use or_insert_with when building the value costs something, because the argument of or_insert is evaluated on every call.
  • entry takes the key by value, so with String keys and borrowed input you build a String even on a hit.
  • If you only read, or only change keys that already exist, use get or get_mut.
  • A miss makes room for one more item before it returns, even if you then insert nothing.
01

The short answer

counts.entry(word) returns an Entry: an enum that is either Occupied (the key is there) or Vacant (it is not). Both hold a mutable borrow of the map and remember the result of the search. or_insert(0) handles both cases and returns &mut V.

entry alone inserts nothing. Something has to be called on the Entry.

VacantEntry::key
pub fn key(&self) -> &K		read the key you passed in, for example to build the value1.10.0
VacantEntry::into_key
pub fn into_key(self) -> K		take the key back and insert nothing1.12.0
VacantEntry::insert_entry
pub fn insert_entry(self, value: V) -> OccupiedEntry<'a, K, V>		fill the slot and keep an OccupiedEntry1.83.0
02

Common tasks

All of these are in the lab and tested there. Counting is shown above.

Group values by key

Keep the best value per key

and_modify runs only on a hit. It does not also run on the value that or_insert has just added.

Nested maps

Remove, or branch on both cases

Match on the enum when a hit and a miss need different logic. Here a count that reaches zero removes the key.

Import the enum with use std::collections::hash_map::Entry;.

Build a value that can fail

The fallible methods are unstable, so match. The ? leaves before anything is inserted.

String keys with borrowed input

If most calls are hits, look up with the &str first and build the String only on a miss.

A miss now searches twice. A hit searches once and allocates nothing. The shorter counts.entry(word.to_owned()) is fine when most keys are new, or when you already own the String and can move it in.

Memoise a recursive function

You cannot recurse inside or_insert_with, because the entry already borrows the map. Look up, compute, then insert.

03

Pitfalls

Work that happens on every call

Watch out

or_insert(expensive()) always calls expensive(). It is an ordinary argument, evaluated before the method runs, hit or miss. Write or_insert_with(expensive) or or_insert_with(|| ...). Tested here: three calls evaluate the or_insert argument three times and run the closure once.

Watch out

entry(word.to_owned()) allocates on every call. get accepts any borrowed form of the key (&str for String keys). entry takes K itself. Tested here with a counting allocator: 100 hits cost 100 allocations through entry, and none through get_mut.

The closure cannot use the map

This does not compile (E0502):

Read what you need into a local before you call entry: let n = m.len();.

Returning early from get_mut is rejected

You might try to avoid both the extra allocation and the extra look-up like this. Rustc 1.98.1 rejects it with E0499, although the return means the two borrows never overlap when it runs.

The NLL RFC calls this shape "problem case #3". The version below compiles. It pays for one or two extra searches and allocates only on a miss.

A miss can grow the map even if you insert nothing

When the key is absent, entry reserves room for one item before it returns the VacantEntry. On a full table that means growing, even if you then drop the entry. In the lab, a map created with with_capacity(3) and filled up goes from capacity 3 to 7 after let _ = map.entry(new_key);. The test asserts only that capacity grows; 7 is what this toolchain printed.

This matters if you use entry just to check for a key while relying on the map not to reallocate. Use get or contains_key to check.

The map keeps its old key

On a hit, the key you passed is dropped and the stored key stays, even after insert_entry. This only shows when two keys are equal but not identical, such as a case-insensitive key type. Tested here.

Do not assert that capacity() stays the same

The docs promise only that capacity() is a lower bound on what fits without reallocating, and removing items can lower it. Which removals do so depends on where keys landed. The default hasher is randomly seeded, so a test that expects an unchanged capacity can pass in one run and fail in the next. An earlier version of the cookbook's HashMap recipe did exactly that. Assert >= against what you need, never == against an old reading.

The lab forces the effect: every key gets the same hash, 64 go in, 32 come out, and capacity() ends below its starting value.

Why capacity can drophashbrown 0.17.1

Here capacity() is len plus the free room left. Removing an item can leave a "deleted" marker that does not give its room back. clear and drain reset the markers.

04

When not to use entry

Situation Better Why
read only get needs only &self, takes a borrowed key, and never reserves space
update existing keys only get_mut takes a borrowed key; a miss cannot grow the map
overwrite regardless insert says what you mean, and returns the old value
borrowed key, mostly hits get_mut, then insert on a miss no allocation on a hit
the value needs the rest of the map get, compute, insert an Entry holds the only borrow of the map

Not stable in 1.98.1, outside the Entry types: HashMap::try_insert (map_try_insert), and HashSet::entry and get_or_insert_with (hash_set_entry). The std hash map source has no raw_entry method.

Note

The hashbrown crate, which std's map is built on, has entry_ref: it takes a borrowed key and makes the owned one only if you insert. std's HashMap does not offer it. This comes from reading the hashbrown 0.17.1 source; the lab does not use the crate.

05

What it costs

The claim often made for entry is "one look-up instead of two". The lab checks it without a stopwatch, using a BuildHasher that counts how often the map starts a hash. The map has spare room, so nothing is rehashed, and holds one other key, because an empty map can answer a look-up without hashing.

Operation Hashes
*m.entry(k).or_insert(0) += 1, miss 1
the same, hit 1
contains_key, then insert, then get_mut (miss) 3
get_mut, hit 1
get_mut, then insert (miss) 2
Tip

Clippy's clippy::map_entry lint suggests entry where it sees contains_key followed by insert (Clippy 1.98 flagged the lab's three-call test). With a borrowed String key, weigh the suggestion against the allocation described under Pitfalls.

Note

This counts hashes, not time. No timing was measured for this page. How much a saved hash matters depends on the key, the hasher and the hit rate, so measure your own workload before you restructure code for it. On a hit, get_mut and entry both hash once; with String keys the difference is the allocation.

06

How it works

In Rust

Return the result of a check as a value. entry does not return a bool. It returns an enum whose variants hold what the search found, plus the &mut borrow of the map. Only VacantEntry has into_key, only OccupiedEntry has remove, and while either one is alive no other code can change the map, so the answer cannot go stale. The methods that consume self stop you using a slot after it is gone. You can copy this shape whenever "check, then act" must not be split.

A miss through or_insert, and why entry reserves roomfrom hashbrown's rustc_entry.rs
  1. entry hashes the key and searches the table.
  2. The key is absent, so entry reserves room for one item. This is where the table may grow.
  3. The VacantEntry keeps the hash, the owned key and the borrow of the table. Nothing is inserted yet.
  4. or_insert writes with the saved hash: no second hash and no growth check.

Growing a table means rehashing its items, which needs the map's hasher. std's Entry type has no type parameter for the hasher, so VacantEntry::insert cannot do the growing. A comment in the source says that reserving in insert would be better, but adding that parameter to Entry would be a breaking change. This is an implementation detail, not a documented promise.

Cow: borrow until you must own

Cow<'a, B> is an enum that holds either a borrowed &'a B or an owned value, so a function can return its input untouched in the common case and allocate only when it has to change something.

9sections
380lines you can run
14tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
IN 60 SECONDS
  • Return Cow<'a, str> when most inputs come out unchanged and the rest need a new String.
  • Callers use it like a &str, because Cow implements Deref.
  • to_mut clones a borrowed value as soon as you call it, so check whether you need to write first.
  • into_owned gives you the owned value: it moves if already owned and copies if borrowed.
  • A borrowed Cow keeps its source borrowed; Cow<'static, str> holds literals and built strings with no such tie.
  • If you nearly always change the data, return String; if you never do, take and return &str.
01

The pattern

Look for the first thing that needs changing. If there is none, hand the input back. Otherwise build a new value.

  • The signature says "this is your input, or a new string". The '_ ties the result to input.
  • Clean input comes back as the same bytes, with no allocation. Both are tested here.
  • No wasted work on the clean prefix: the search stops at the first special character, and the part before it is copied in one go.
  • The caller usually does not care which variant it got: out.len(), out.starts_with("a") and out == "x" all work.

Cow is short for "clone on write". The type is this:

Common methods

MethodUse whenSince
Cow::into_owned
pub fn into_owned(self) -> <B as ToOwned>::Owned		you need the owned value: moves it if already owned, copies if borrowed1.0.0
Cow::to_mut
pub fn to_mut(&mut self) -> &mut <B as ToOwned>::Owned		you are about to change the data: copies a borrowed value as soon as you call it1.0.0
All 4 methodsfull list
MethodUse whenSince
Cow::into_owned

Cow::to_mut
pub fn to_mut(&mut self) -> &mut <B as ToOwned>::Owned		you are about to change the data: copies a borrowed value as soon as you call it1.0.0
Cow::is_borrowed

Cow::is_owned

02

Should you use it?

Use Cow when Do something else when
most calls need no change, some do (escaping, normalising, lossy decoding) nearly every call changes the data: return String
a value is usually a string literal and sometimes formatted it is always a literal: use &'static str
a struct is usually filled from a buffer that outlives it, and sometimes from computed text the struct must be stored or sent around freely: use String
a function sometimes has to change a value it was lent it only reads: take &str
it always needs to own the value: take String, and let the caller decide whether to clone
it runs in a loop and the caller can reuse a buffer: write into &mut String

The last two are alternatives that are easy to miss. The Rust API Guidelines (C-CALLER-CONTROL) say a function that needs ownership should take ownership, not borrow and clone. And a caller-owned buffer can avoid allocating even for input that changes:

In the lab, escaping dirty input three times into one buffer with enough room makes no allocation. The Cow version allocates for each dirty input.

Tip

Before choosing Cow, estimate how often the borrowed path will be taken on real input. That share is the whole benefit. This is advice; it was not measured here.

03

Compared with &str and String

&'a str String Cow<'a, str>
owns its text no yes sometimes
has a lifetime yes no yes ('static is allowed)
can hold newly built text no, someone else must own it yes yes
holding existing text without a copy yes only by moving a String in yes
can be changed no yes through to_mut
size on this toolchain 16 bytes 24 bytes 24 bytes

The sizes were printed by the lab on 64-bit aarch64-apple-darwin with rustc 1.98.1. Rust does not guarantee the layout of these types. Here, storing Cow instead of String saved no space inline.

04

Working with a Cow

Operation On Borrowed On Owned
call a &str method (through Deref) no copy no copy
to_mut() gives &mut String copies, and becomes Owned no copy
into_owned() gives String copies moves
clone() copies the reference copies the data
to_string() copies copies
==, ordering, hashing by content by content

The lab counts allocations for into_owned on both variants, clone on both, and to_string on an owned value. The other cells follow from the source.

Making one. Cow::Borrowed(s) and Cow::Owned(string) name the variant. From does the obvious thing: &str and &String become Borrowed, and a String is moved into Owned without a copy.

Asking which one you have. On stable, use matches!(c, Cow::Borrowed(_)).

Changing it only when needed

to_mut is lazy only in the sense that it does nothing to a value that is already owned. It cannot know whether you are about to change anything.

Writing through to_mut never touches the borrowed source. It changes the new copy.

05

In structs and signatures

A field that borrows when it can

  • Label<'a> cannot outlive whatever it borrows. The lifetime spreads to every type that contains a Label<'a>. That is the main design cost.
  • into_static is the way out at a boundary, such as before caching the value or moving it to a spawned thread. Cow has into_owned, which returns a String; it has no method that returns Cow<'static, str>, so you wrap the result in Cow::Owned.
  • impl Into<Cow<'a, str>> suits a constructor that stores the value. A function that only reads should just take &str.

Literals and built strings: Cow<'static, str>

A string literal has type &'static str, so borrowing it ties the result to nothing. The caller can keep the value as long as it likes, and the known cases do not allocate.

Slices work the same way

As a map key

A HashMap<Cow<'static, str>, V> can hold literals and built strings together, and map.get("name") works, because Cow<str> implements Borrow<str>. A borrowed key and an owned key with the same text are the same key. Tested here.

06

What it costs

Cost Detail
a lifetime a Cow<'a, _> that may borrow keeps its source alive and unchanged while you hold it
two cases Deref matches on the variant each time it runs (see the source). Its run-time cost was not measured
a check before building you must find out whether a change is needed; arrange it so that work is not repeated, as escape_html does
API surface Cow in a public signature is something every caller has to read and understand

What you get is fewer allocations on the borrowed path. The lab counts them: zero for clean input to escape_html, a known code in status_text, sorted input to sorted, and valid UTF-8 in from_utf8_lossy; one for escape_html("a<b").

Note

No timing was measured for this page. Fewer allocations is not the same as a faster program: profile before you add a lifetime to your types for speed.

07

Pitfalls

Getting the owned value out

Watch out

cow.to_owned() does not give you a String. Cow is Clone, and every Clone type implements ToOwned with Owned = Self. So this clones the Cow, and a borrowed one stays borrowed. Use into_owned(). Clippy 1.98 warns about it (clippy::suspicious_to_owned, seen on the lab's test).

Watch out

to_string() always makes a new String, even when the Cow already owns one. into_owned() moves it out. The lab checks this by comparing buffer addresses.

from_utf8_lossy on bytes you already own

String::from_utf8_lossy takes &[u8]. For valid input it borrows from your Vec, so calling into_owned() on the result copies bytes you already had. Try String::from_utf8 first; it takes the Vec and reuses its buffer.

(String::from_utf8_lossy_owned does this job but is unstable in 1.98.1.)

Owned does not mean "changed"

The variant says who owns the data, not whether it differs from the input. Cow::Owned can hold text equal to the original, and == compares text only. If callers need a "was it changed?" answer, design for it, and document what your function promises about the variant.

The result keeps the input borrowed

Neither of these compiles. The first returns a borrow of a local (E0515). Return Cow::Owned(upper) instead.

The second changes the source while a borrowed Cow is still in use (E0502).

This bites when one buffer is reused to read line after line: call into_owned() on anything you keep past the next read.

serde does not borrow a Cow unless you ask

With serde's derive, a Cow<'a, str> field is deserialized as Owned unless it is marked #[serde(borrow)].

Checked in a scratch project with serde 1.0.229 and serde_json 1.0.154, using from_str: without the attribute the field was Owned; with it, {"name":"abc"} gave Borrowed; with it, a string containing the escape \n gave Owned, because the decoded text is not in the input. Not every input can lend data: serde's docs give reading from an IO stream as an example. The fence above is not compiled by the page checker, because it needs the serde dependency, which the lab does not have.

08

Where std and crates use it

Function Returns Borrowed when Returns Owned when
String::from_utf8_lossy(&[u8]) the bytes are valid UTF-8 invalid sequences are replaced with U+FFFD
CStr::to_string_lossy the same (it calls from_utf8_lossy) the same
OsStr::to_string_lossy the name is valid Unicode it is not
Path::to_string_lossy the path is valid Unicode it is not
Regex::replace_all (regex crate) there is no match there is at least one match

The std rows are tested here for valid input, and for invalid input except through Path, with the OsStr invalid case on Unix only. Windows was not run. The regex row comes from reading the 1.13.2 source (replacen, which replace_all is built on) and was not run.

How from_utf8_lossy decidesalloc/src/string.rs

It checks the first chunk of the input. If that chunk has no invalid bytes, it is the whole input, and the function returns it as Borrowed without allocating. Only past that point does it create a String.

09

How it is built

ToOwned, and why Owned must borrow as Selfalloc/src/borrow.rs

Cow has to name two types: the borrowed one (str) and the owned one (String). Clone cannot express that, since it goes from &T to T, and str is unsized. The ToOwned trait links the two:

The bound Owned: Borrow<Self> is what makes Deref possible: from either variant, Cow can produce a &B. In the Owned case it calls borrow().

In Rust

An associated type plus a bound back to Self lets a generic type work with pairs such as str/String, [T]/Vec<T> and Path/PathBuf without knowing any of them. to_mut is also worth reading in the source: when borrowed, it assigns a new Owned value to *self and then matches again to return a reference into it.

Aside

For clone-on-write between several owners, the Cow docs point to Rc::make_mut and Arc::make_mut. They solve a different problem: shared ownership, with no borrowed variant and no lifetime tying the value to someone else's data.

RUST LANGUAGE · COMPARISON

Choosing an error type

Four ways to fill the E in Result<T, E>: a hand-written enum, the same enum derived with thiserror, anyhow::Error, and Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>. The choice depends mostly on whether callers need to act differently on different failures.

8sections
518lines you can run
13tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
IN 60 SECONDS
  • If callers must react differently to different failures, return your own type, usually an enum.
  • thiserror writes the same Display and Error code you would write by hand, and does not appear in your public API.
  • If an application only reports the failure, anyhow::Error gives you context and a printable cause chain with little code.
  • Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> needs no dependency, but adding context means writing your own wrapper type.
  • Put each cause either in the message or in source(), never both.
  • With a type-erased error, finding a cause by type can silently return nothing after some conversions and wrappers.
01

Which one to use

Ask these questions in order. The recommendations are advice; the properties behind them are shown further down.

Your situation Use Main cost
A library, or any boundary where a caller branches on the failure; dependencies are fine An enum with thiserror You design and maintain the variants
The same, but you want no dependencies (or no proc macro) A hand-written enum Display, source() and any From impls by hand
An application, or its top layers, where failures are reported to a person or a log anyhow::Error The signature no longer says what can fail
The same, but no dependencies, or a small tool, example or test helper Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> No context method, no ready-made chain report

Library or application is a shortcut for the real question: will code that you do not control, or code far away, need to tell the failures apart? A library usually cannot know, so give it a concrete type. An internal module of an application may know that nobody will ever match, and then erasing the type is fine.

The authors draw the same line. The thiserror README recommends it when the caller should get exactly the information you choose, which is most often library code. It recommends anyhow when you do not care which error type your functions return, which is common in application code.

Mixing them is normal. A common shape: library crates return enums, and the binary collects them into anyhow::Error with context.

Tip

Do not return anyhow::Error from a public library function "for now". Changing it to an enum later breaks every caller.

02

Side by side

Property Hand-written enum thiserror enum anyhow::Error Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>
Signature says what can fail Yes Yes No No
Caller tells failures apart with match match downcast at run time downcast at run time
Compiler checks the arms Yes Yes No No
? accepts another error type When you write From With #[from] Any Error + Send + Sync + 'static Any Error + Send + Sync, String, &str
Add context New variant or field New variant or field .context(..), .with_context(..) Write a wrapper type
Attach data a caller can read Fields Fields Only by downcasting to a type that has it Same
Print the cause chain Walk source() Walk source() {:#} or {:?} Walk source()
Backtrace What you add A Backtrace field (needs nightly) Captured when enabled by RUST_BACKTRACE or RUST_LIB_BACKTRACE None added
Implements std::error::Error Yes Yes No No (see Moving between them)
Dependency None thiserror anyhow None

When you do not match on variants, the two enum columns and the two erased columns behave much alike. The large step is between a concrete type and an erased one.

API stability. Switching between a hand-written impl and thiserror is not a breaking change, because the macro does not appear in your public API (thiserror docs). Adding a variant to a public enum is breaking unless it was marked #[non_exhaustive], which makes other crates keep a wildcard arm. A source field whose type comes from a dependency also makes that dependency part of your API (advice: if that matters, wrap the enum in an opaque public struct; the thiserror docs show how with #[error(transparent)]).

03

The same task, four ways

Read a file, find its port= line, return the port. Four things can go wrong: the file cannot be read, the line is missing, the value is not a u16, or it is 0. The lab's tests check that all four versions give the same messages.

Hand-written enum

You write the type, its Display and its source().

The same enum with thiserror

A field named source, or marked #[source] or #[from], becomes the cause.

The functions that return either enum are identical. Each failure is converted with map_err, because the variant needs data (path, text) that ? alone cannot supply:

In Rust

#[from] lets ? convert on its own, but a #[from] variant can hold nothing except the source (and a backtrace). So it cannot keep the path. It also allows only one such variant per source type: a second one is a conflicting From impl (E0119). Use #[from] when the source type alone says what happened.

anyhow

No type to declare. context adds a layer, with_context builds its message only on failure, and both also work on Option.

Box of dyn Error

? boxes any error, and &str or String convert into an error that is only a message. std has no method that adds context, so the file defines one wrapper. Writing map_err(|e| format!("cannot read ..: {e}")) instead is shorter, but it throws the cause away as a value.

Include Send + Sync + 'static. Without Send the error cannot cross threads, and anyhow requires all three. The API Guidelines also ask for error types to be Error + Send + Sync, with messages in lowercase without trailing punctuation.

04

Context and sources

Error::source() returns the cause below an error. Following it gives a chain, from "what I was doing" down to the root cause.

Watch out

An error should either return its cause from source() or include it in its Display text, not both (std Error docs). A type that does both prints the cause twice in any report that walks the chain. The lab shows storage failed: disk gone: disk gone.

So Display on one error shows one layer. println!("{e}") on any of the four loses the reason. Print the chain at the place where you report:

For the missing file, all four versions then print the same line (from cargo run on macOS; the last part comes from the operating system):

anyhow has the reports built in. This is the lab's output for port=eighty, without a backtrace:

Format Output
{} invalid port "eighty"
{:#} invalid port "eighty": invalid digit found in string
{:?} The message, then a Caused by: list on later lines, then a backtrace if one was captured
{:#?} A struct-like debug dump

What fn main prints

When main returns Err, std prints Error: followed by the Debug form and exits with failure (read in std/src/process.rs). What you get depends on the type:

Error type Debug form
A derived-Debug enum Error: Zero
A boxed &str Error: "port must not be 0"
anyhow::Error The readable multi-line report

So fn main() -> anyhow::Result<()> gives good output for free. With the other types, call your own run() from main and format the chain yourself.

Context wording (advice): say what this layer was trying to do and with which input (cannot read /etc/app.conf). Do not repeat the cause, and do not add a layer that says only "error occurred".

05

Matching and downcasting

With an enum, matching is ordinary Rust, and the variant's fields come with it:

With an erased type you downcast: you ask "is there a value of type T in here?" The answer is an Option, and a wrong guess about the type compiles. The three calls look alike and search different things:

Call Looks at
anyhow_error.downcast_ref::<T>() The original error and every context value added with anyhow's context
dyn_error.downcast_ref::<T>() (std) Only the outermost value's concrete type
Walking source() and downcasting each Every error that appears in the chain, by its concrete type

anyhow documents that a downcast that worked before you added context still works afterwards (Context, effect on downcasting). That promise is about anyhow::Error's own methods. Several things below fall outside it.

Why anyhow's downcast can see more than std'sinternals, anyhow 1.0.105

context stores the context value and the earlier error together in a private wrapper type. anyhow::Error keeps its own table of functions for each stored value. The downcast function for a context wrapper checks the context's type, then the wrapped error's type, and for stacked context it recurses downward (context_downcast and context_chain_downcast in src/error.rs).

A &dyn std::error::Error view has none of that. Its concrete type is the private wrapper, so a std downcast to your type fails. Walking source() reaches your original error one step down. It never reaches a context value, because a context value is not an error in the chain: it only supplies the wrapper's message.

06

Exit codes and HTTP statuses

Decide exit codes and statuses in one place, at the edge of the program, not inside the library that failed (advice). The same error can mean different things to different programs.

The numbers are this example's policy, not a standard. What matters:

  • Inside the crate that defines the enum, this match has no wildcard, so a new variant does not compile until someone gives it a status. (#[non_exhaustive] only forces the wildcard on other crates.)
  • A message that is safe for a log may leak paths or queries to a client. Send a fixed text for server errors.
  • A read failure is not one thing: io::Error::kind() separates "not found" from the rest.

With anyhow, the mapping depends on a downcast, so it needs a fallback, and a broken downcast lands there without any warning:

Testing

Test the mapping through the real call path, with the context and conversions production uses. A test that builds the error directly would not notice that a later conversion turned every 422 into a 500.

For a command-line program, return ExitCode from main so that destructors run. process::exit ends the process without running them.

07

Moving between them

What ? can convert

From Into Does ? work? Can you still downcast to your type?
Your enum anyhow::Error Yes Yes
Your enum Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> Yes Yes
anyhow::Error Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> Yes No
Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync> anyhow::Error No, compile error E0277 After from_boxed: not directly
anyhow::Error Your enum With a variant Other(#[from] anyhow::Error) Match the variant first

The surprising row is the fourth. A box of dyn Error does not implement Error: std implements Error for Box<E> only when E has a known size, and dyn Error does not. anyhow's From impl needs Error. The cause fits in a few lines of plain std, which the checker compiles to confirm the error:

With anyhow, lib()?; on such a result gives `?` couldn't convert the error: `dyn std::error::Error + Send + Sync: Sized` is not satisfied (rustc 1.98.1, tried in a scratch crate). Convert with .map_err(anyhow::Error::from_boxed), and read the first two pitfalls below. If the library is yours, return a concrete type and the problem goes away.

08

Pitfalls

Each of these is a passing test in tests/pitfalls.rs, with anyhow 1.0.105 and thiserror 2.0.21.

Boxing an anyhow error

Turning anyhow::Error into a boxed std error, with ? or .into(), keeps the message and loses the downcast, even with no context at all.

In the source, the ordinary conversion boxes anyhow's whole internal record, so the concrete type is that record. reallocate_into_boxed_dyn_error_without_backtrace moves your value into a new box. It keeps the type of what anyhow holds, so if you added context, that is still the context wrapper and you must walk the chain.

from_boxed hides the type

anyhow::Error::from_boxed stores the box. Downcasting to your type fails, on the error and along chain(). The same happens with anyhow!(boxed) (checked in a scratch crate). You can only ask for the box, then look inside it:

Viewing anyhow as a std error

After .context(..), passing the error to code that takes &dyn Error (through as_ref()) and calling downcast_ref there finds nothing. Walk the chain instead.

Searching the chain for a context type

If you attach a type as context in order to match on it later, only anyhow::Error::downcast_ref finds it. A generic reporter or middleware that walks chain() does not.

Formatting the cause into a message

anyhow!(error) keeps the error. anyhow!("startup failed: {}", error) builds a new message-only error: the type and the chain are gone. The same is true of map_err(|e| format!(..)). Use .context("startup failed").

transparent removes a link

#[error(transparent)] forwards both Display and source() to the inner error. The wrapper therefore replaces the inner error in the chain: source() returns the inner error's source, not the inner error. A chain walk for the inner type finds nothing. Matching the variant still works.

Two versions of one crate

A downcast compares exact types. If your dependency tree holds two incompatible versions of the crate that defines the error, their types are different and the downcast misses (this follows from how Cargo builds each version separately; not tested here). cargo tree -d lists duplicates.

Not checked: Run here: build, tests, clippy, rustfmt and cargo run. CONCURRENCY AND ASYNC · CONCEPT

Acquire and release ordering

A Release store and an Acquire load that reads it create a promise between two threads: everything the writer did before the store is visible to the reader after the load. This is how ordinary data is handed from one thread to another through one atomic.

10sections
469lines you can run
5tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
Where it sits
  1. Hardware
  2. Compiler
  3. Rust memory model
  4. Atomic types
  5. Mutex, channel, Arc
IN 60 SECONDS
  • Use Release on the write that says "my data is ready" and Acquire on the read that checks it.
  • The promise exists only if the Acquire side reads the value that the Release side wrote (or a later one that continues it).
  • Relaxed keeps each atomic operation whole, but orders nothing around it, so it cannot hand over other data.
  • Neither acquire nor release stops two threads from each storing a flag and then both missing the other's: that needs SeqCst.
  • A test on real threads that passes thousands of times does not show that an ordering is strong enough.
  • Tested here: four ordering bugs on ordinary data passed all 20 native test runs, while Miri (all 32 seeds tried) and loom caught each one.
01

When you need it

You need acquire and release when one thread must see other memory that another thread wrote, and an atomic is how it finds out that the memory is ready.

What the atomic is for Ordering
A counter or id generator that carries no other data Relaxed
"The data is ready": writer side store(.., Release)
"Is the data ready?": reader side load(Acquire)
A lock Acquire to take it, Release to unlock
Read-modify-write that does both jobs AcqRel
Each thread writes its own flag, then reads the other's SeqCst
You are not sure A Mutex or a channel (advice)

The main cost is not speed. It is that a wrong choice usually compiles, passes its tests and fails rarely. Prefer Mutex, a channel or OnceLock unless you have a reason to build on atomics (advice).

You do not need it when something else already orders the two threads. For example, join promises that everything the thread did happens before join returns. So a counter that you read only after joining its writers can be Relaxed.

02

Happens-before in plain words

Threads do not share one agreed timeline. The compiler may reorder your memory operations when one thread could not tell the difference, and a processor may make writes visible to other cores in a different order.

Happens-before is the order the language does promise. If a write happens before a read, the read sees that write (or a later one). Inside one thread, program order gives you this. Between two threads you get it only from specific synchronizing operations.

This matters beyond stale values. The standard library's memory model says that two accesses to the same memory are a data race if at least one writes, at least one is non-atomic, and neither happens before the other. A data race is undefined behaviour. It is not "you might read the old value".

Release and acquire add one edge between threads:

  1. Thread A writes some data.
  2. Thread A stores to an atomic x with Release.
  3. Thread B loads x with Acquire and reads the value A stored.
  4. Now everything A did before step 2 happens before everything B does after step 3.
Watch out

Step 3 is a condition, not a formality. If B's load returns the old value, there is no edge at all, and B must not touch the data. An Acquire load does not wait for anything.

The one-way fences are a useful picture, with limits. Earlier accesses cannot move after a release. Later accesses cannot move before an acquire. The fence documentation warns that "preventing reordering" is a simplified model. When you argue that code is correct, argue with happens-before edges.

03

Publishing data

The classic use is publication, also called message passing: write ordinary data once, then let one flag hand it over. The data here is a plain UnsafeCell<u64>, not an atomic. Only the flag's ordering makes the read legal.

Two parts of the design make the unsafe sound, and the ordering is only one of them. publish takes self and there is one Publisher, so safe code cannot write twice. A reader never reads before it has seen the flag.

In Rust

UnsafeCell is not Sync, so the type needs unsafe impl Sync. That line is where you take over the compiler's job. Write the happens-before argument next to it, as publish.rs does. The with and with_mut closures copy the shape of loom's UnsafeCell, so one source file builds for both.

Without that unsafe impl, sharing the cell between threads does not compile. The checker compiles this snippet to confirm the error:

04

Why Relaxed is not enough

Relaxed operations are still atomic: no torn values, and a read-modify-write such as fetch_add loses no updates. They create no happens-before edge, so they cannot make other memory visible.

To try this without undefined behaviour, the lab has a mailbox whose message is also an atomic. A weak flag can then give a wrong value, but never a data race.

With Release and Acquire on the flag, a stale read is impossible. With Relaxed on either side it is allowed. One matching side is not enough.

Measured here. cargo run --release sends 100,000 mailboxes between two threads. Over 20 runs, the Relaxed/Relaxed version saw between 124 and 295 stale reads per run, and the Release/Acquire version saw none. (Apple M4 Pro, macOS 27.0, rustc 1.98.1, 2026-11-26.) The run does not show whether the compiler or the processor caused the reordering. The counts depend on this loop and this machine. Under Miri, one run saw 49 stale reads in 100 rounds.

Why x86 hides this

These are single operations compiled on their own with rustc -O 1.98.1 (tested here, from the emitted assembly):

Operation aarch64 (Apple target) x86-64
load(Relaxed) ldr mov
load(Acquire) ldapr mov
load(SeqCst) ldar mov
store(Relaxed) str mov
store(Release) stlr mov
store(SeqCst) stlr xchg

On x86-64, Relaxed and Release/Acquire produced the same instructions here. The x86 hardware model (total store order) already forbids the message-passing reordering between two plain stores and two plain loads, while ARM and POWER allow it (Russ Cox, Hardware Memory Models).

So a missing Release can look correct on every x86 machine you try. It is still wrong, for two reasons. The compiler works from the Rust model, not from x86, and may reorder around a Relaxed operation even when the target processor would not. And the same source may later run on ARM. The Rustonomicon advises testing concurrent algorithms on weakly ordered hardware.

Note

The table shows isolated operations. It says nothing about how the compiler moves the code around them, and it was not run on x86 hardware.

05

Last one out: reference counting

Publication has one writer and a flag. The second common pattern has several threads that finish with some shared data, and the last one to finish uses all of it, often to destroy it. A reference count is this pattern.

The lab strips it down: two owners each write a result, then count down. The one that reaches zero reads both.

  • Every thread decrements with Release, because any of them may not be last, and its work must be visible to whoever is.
  • Only the last thread needs the Acquire. A separate fence lets the others skip it. The fence docs describe this "atomic to fence" pairing: a release operation, then, on the other thread, any read of that atomic followed by an acquire fence.
  • Using fetch_sub(1, AcqRel) instead would also be correct. It asks for acquire on every decrement.

What Arc does

Arc uses this pattern: clone increments with Relaxed, and drop decrements with Release, then the last owner runs an Acquire fence before destroying the value.

The orderings in Arc, and the source's reasonsrustc 1.98.1

Read in the standard library source, alloc/src/sync.rs:

Operation Ordering The source's reason
Arc::clone strong.fetch_add(1, Relaxed) You already hold a reference, so the object cannot be destroyed meanwhile. Handing the new reference to another thread must already synchronize.
Drop for Arc strong.fetch_sub(1, Release); if it was the last, an Acquire fence, then destroy All use of the data through any reference must happen before the deletion.
Drop for Weak The same shape on the weak count Same reason, for freeing the allocation.

The comment in drop gives a case that shows why this matters: the value may be something like a Mutex<T>. Destroying it does not lock the mutex, so the lock cannot be what makes another thread's writes visible to the destructor.

The same file has a detail worth knowing: under ThreadSanitizer, which does not support fences, the fence is replaced by an Acquire load of the counter.

In production

clone also aborts the process if the count passes isize::MAX. Ordering is one part of a correct reference count. Overflow, weak references and uniqueness checks are others. Use Arc (advice).

06

When SeqCst matters

Here two threads each store their own flag, then load the other's. Old mutual-exclusion algorithms such as Dekker's depend on at least one of them seeing the other.

Thread 1 Thread 2
left = 1 right = 1
a = right b = left

Can both a and b be 0?

Orderings Both zero allowed?
Release stores, Acquire loads Yes
All four accesses SeqCst No
Relaxed accesses with fence(SeqCst) between each store and load No

Release and acquire do not help, because neither load needs to read the other thread's store. If a load returns 0, it read the initial value, so no edge was created. Nothing orders one thread's store before its later load of a different location.

SeqCst adds the guarantee that all threads agree on one order of all SeqCst operations (Ordering). In that order, one of the two stores comes first, so the other thread's later load must see it. This happens on x86 too: its stores wait in a per-core queue, so both loads can run before either store is visible (Russ Cox). That is why the table above shows xchg for the x86 SeqCst store.

Watch out

Making one operation SeqCst does not make the others safe. The single order covers SeqCst operations and fences only. In this test, both threads need it on both sides: keeping the stores SeqCst and weakening only the loads to Acquire let both threads read 0 under Miri, on all 32 seeds tried (tested here).

The Rustonomicon says SeqCst is rarely needed for correctness, but is the right choice if you are unsure about the weaker orderings. Treat that as a starting point, not a repair: SeqCst on a wrong algorithm is still wrong.

07

What testing can find

Each row below is a deliberate bug put into a scratch copy of the lab, one at a time. This is the most useful table on the page.

  • Real threads: cargo test --release --test threads, run 20 times. The number is how many runs failed.
  • Miri: the one relevant test, with 32 seeds (-Zmiri-seed=0 to 31). The number is how many seeds failed.
  • loom: tests/model.rs, one run.
Bug Real threads Miri loom
Publication: store Release to Relaxed 0 of 20 32 of 32 (data race) caught
Publication: load Acquire to Relaxed 0 of 20 32 of 32 (data race) caught
Countdown: decrement Release to Relaxed 0 of 20 32 of 32 (data race) caught
Countdown: Acquire fence removed 0 of 20 32 of 32 (data race) caught
Mailbox test made Relaxed/Relaxed (atomics only) 13 of 20 32 of 32 caught (separate tests, one side weak each)
Store buffering: fence(SeqCst) removed 2 of 20 32 of 32 caught
Store buffering: SeqCst accesses to Release/Acquire 0 of 20 32 of 32 cannot tell them apart

What this shows.

  • All four bugs on ordinary data, each of which is undefined behaviour, passed every native run, on ARM hardware that allows the reordering. The tests that did this are in the lab and they pass. They check behaviour; they do not check the orderings.
  • Two bugs were caught natively only sometimes. A flaky failure like that is easy to retry and forget.
  • The counts describe these tiny programs, these tests and this machine. "32 of 32" is not a detection rate you can expect elsewhere.

Why passing many times proves little

A stress test samples whatever your processor, compiler and scheduler happen to do. A bug needs a particular interleaving and a particular reordering in a narrow window. A loop that starts two new threads each round gives them little chance to overlap (a likely reason for the zeros, not investigated). The mailbox loop, where the reader chases the writer, exposed far more. Changing the target, the compiler version or an unrelated line can change what you see. On x86, one whole class of reordering does not happen in hardware at all.

Tip

To test a concurrency test, weaken an ordering in a scratch copy and see what fails. If nothing does, your test is not what protects that ordering. A review with a written happens-before argument, Miri or loom has to. Never commit the weakened ordinary-data version, and give each mutated copy its own --target-dir.

08

Miri

Miri interprets your program and reports undefined behaviour, including data races. It also emulates some weak memory effects: an atomic load can return an outdated value even where your processor would not show it.

This is the real output (shortened) for the first bug in the table, a Relaxed publication store:

Miri reports the missing happens-before edge. The read did not have to return a wrong value.

On the unchanged lab, cargo miri test passes, and so do 32 seeds of the thread tests.

What it cannot do, from its README:

  • It runs one execution per seed. It misses bugs that appear only in another one. More seeds help but do not explore them all.
  • Its weak memory emulation is incomplete: some legal behaviours never appear.
  • It only checks the code your tests run. A clean run is not a proof of soundness.
  • It does not support most platform APIs and FFI, and it is much slower than native code. The lab uses smaller loop counts under cfg(miri).
09

loom

loom is a library. You write a small test inside loom::model, and it runs the closure again and again, exploring the thread interleavings and values that its model of the C11 memory model allows. Its UnsafeCell reports unsynchronized access.

It sees only its own types. Your code must use loom's atomics, cells and threads under a --cfg loom build:

The lab's Run and Test buttons do not run these: without the flag, the file compiles to no tests. With a weakened publication ordering, loom 0.7.3 failed with Causality violation: Concurrent read and write accesses.

Where loom is wrong or blind, from its README and crate docs (0.7.3):

Limit Effect
SeqCst loads and stores are treated as AcqRel False alarms: it reports "both zero" for correct code. fence(SeqCst) is supported. The lab has a test that shows this.
It does not explore load buffering It can miss a real bug.
It cannot model every reordering that Relaxed allows, nor some across different atomics It can miss a real bug.
Only loom types are visible Synchronization inside other libraries is not modelled.
State grows quickly with threads and operations Keep models tiny. LOOM_MAX_PREEMPTIONS bounds the search, which then is no longer exhaustive.
Its scheduler is not fair A spin loop must call loom::thread::yield_now.

So neither tool proves your code correct. They fail in different places: in the table above, Miri separated SeqCst from AcqRel and loom could not, while loom explores schedules systematically where Miri samples them by seed.

10

Pitfalls and tips

Mistake Why it is wrong Instead
Release store, Relaxed load (or the reverse) The edge needs both sides Pair them
Releasing on one atomic and acquiring on another The pairing goes through the value read from one atomic (or through fences around such accesses) Use the same flag
Touching the data when the Acquire load saw the old value No edge was created Branch on the loaded value
Writing the data again after publishing it A reader may be reading it: a data race Publish once, or use a lock
swap(.., Release) expecting the read half to acquire The load half of a Release read-modify-write is Relaxed AcqRel
swap(.., Acquire) expecting the write half to release The store half of an Acquire read-modify-write is Relaxed AcqRel
"I need SeqCst so other threads see it sooner" Ordering says nothing about how soon a value arrives; it orders accesses Choose by what must be ordered
load(Release) or store(.., Acquire) These panic Match the ordering to the operation
Tip

Write the pairing in a comment on both sides: "pairs with the Release store in publish". If you cannot name the partner of an Acquire or Release, you have not finished the argument.

Do the orderings make a thread wait?No

None of these orderings blocks. try_read returns at once with None if the flag is not set. Waiting is a separate job: a loop with spin_loop for very short waits, thread::park, or better a Mutex with a Condvar or a channel (advice). The lab's native loops call yield_now so that they finish when there are more threads than cores.

Terms
happens-beforeThe order between operations that the language guarantees, within and between threads.
data raceConflicting accesses, at least one non-atomic, with no happens-before between them; undefined behaviour.
publicationWriting data once and handing it to other threads through a release store.
litmus testA tiny concurrent program whose possible results show what a memory model allows.
total store orderThe x86 model: each core queues its stores, and all cores agree on the order they reach memory.
fenceAn ordering operation that is not attached to one memory location.
store bufferingBoth threads store, then load the other location, and both read the old value.
