TESTING AND BENCHMARKING · TESTING

Testing unsafe code and finding unsoundness

How to test a safe API that is built on unsafe code: attack it the way hostile safe code could, and run those attacks under tools that can see undefined behaviour.

13sections
799lines you can run
20tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
IN 60 SECONDS
  • A safe API is unsound if some safe code can make it cause undefined behaviour (UB). Code that is only buggy gives wrong results without UB.
  • Write down the invariants your unsafe blocks rely on, and keep them true whenever caller code runs: closures, iterators, destructors.
  • Well-behaved tests are not enough: in the example here, all three planted soundness bugs pass the well-behaved model test, even under Miri.
  • Write hostile tests (lying trait impls, re-entrancy, panics) and run them under Miri, which checks only the executions you give it.
  • You need two kinds of oracle: a model checks answers, while Miri and sanitizers look for UB.
  • Break the code on purpose and require each check to fail for the expected reason.
  • Before you keep the unsafe, compare it with a safe version.
01

Unsound or just wrong

Use this page when a type or function has unsafe inside and a safe signature outside. The main cost of such code: the compiler no longer proves all of that module's memory safety, so you have to argue the rest and test it.

The Rust Reference puts the duty on the author of the unsafe code. It is sound if no safe client can trigger undefined behaviour through it, and unsound if safe code can misuse it into UB (Reference). "No safe client" includes clients that are wrong or deliberately strange.

Buggy but sound Unsound
What goes wrong wrong result, panic, leak, deadlock safe code can reach undefined behaviour
What you can still rely on the language's guarantees nothing about a program that executes the UB
Must your program hit it for it to be a defect? it hurts when it happens no: the API is already broken if some safe caller can do it
What finds it assertions, a model, property tests the same attacks run under a UB detector, plus review
Planted in this page's code planted-wrong-get planted-lying-len, planted-stale-index, planted-early-len

Two consequences are easy to miss:

  • A change to safe code can make unsafe code wrong. The Rustonomicon changes < to <= in the bounds check that guards a get_unchecked. Only safe code changed, and the function became unsound (Working with unsafe). Review all the code that can touch the data an unsafe block depends on.
  • You cannot trust code your caller supplies. Anyone can implement a safe trait such as Ord or ExactSizeIterator wrongly, without writing unsafe. Your type may then give wrong answers, but it must not turn them into UB (How safe and unsafe interact).
Note

Leaking memory is safe in Rust: std::mem::forget is a safe function. A leak is a bug, not unsoundness. It is still a useful alarm, because in unsafe code it often means the bookkeeping is wrong.

02

The example: a small safe wrapper

Shelf<T, N> is a fixed-capacity, append-only list. Its special feature: push takes &self and returns a reference that stays valid while you push more. Vec::push takes &mut self, so the borrow checker does not let you do that with a Vec.

Four invariants are written on the type, and every unsafe block depends on some of them.

Invariant What relies on it
1 len <= N indexing
2 slots 0..len hold a live T; slots len..N hold nothing the shelf owns get reads, clear drops
3 while any &self borrow lives, a slot below len is not written, moved or dropped every reference the shelf hands out
4 only one thread uses &self at a time push has no synchronisation
In Rust

UnsafeCell is what permits mutation through &self. The Reference says memory behind a live &T must not be mutated, except data inside an UnsafeCell. That exception belongs to references to the cell. The &T that get returns points at the contents as a plain T, so overwriting that slot while the reference is live is UB (for a T with no UnsafeCell of its own). Hence invariant 3. The Reference also warns that the exact aliasing rules are not settled.

Three methods run code the shelf did not write: extend_exact consumes a caller's iterator, fill_with calls a caller's closure to make values, and clear runs the elements' destructors.

The crate also has SafeShelf, the same idea built on OnceCell with no unsafe at all. It is a second oracle and the benchmark baseline.

03

Choose the oracle first

An oracle is whatever tells a test that something went wrong. UB has no reliable symptom: the program may crash, give wrong answers or seem to work. One oracle is not enough.

Oracle Catches Blind to Here
A model: a Vec that gets the same operations wrong length, order, contents, return values UB that changes no answer tests/model.rs, src/script.rs
A second implementation without unsafe disagreement between the two mistakes both share src/safe.rs, tests/twin.rs
Held references: keep every &T, re-read all after each operation a value changing under a shared reference damage nobody reads back src/script.rs
A drop ledger: count destructor calls per element double drop, missing drop reads of dead memory script::Ledger
Miri many kinds of UB, and leaks, on the paths that run paths that do not run; wrong answers cargo +nightly miri test
A sanitizer the errors it instruments, in native code other kinds of UB AddressSanitizer
The compiler uses that the types forbid anything about run-time values compile_fail doctests

The model, held references and ledger are ordinary Rust. They work under cargo test and under Miri, and are written so a fuzzer can drive them. The script driver checks them after each operation:

Tip

Give test elements a heap allocation and a destructor (here a String plus a drop counter). With u64 elements there is nothing to leak or double-free, so the memory tools have less to find.

04

Write invariants you can test

A safety comment should say which invariants it relies on and why they hold at this line. "This is fine" cannot be reviewed.

The rule to test is: the invariants hold whenever code you did not write runs. Find each such point. Then ask what happens if that code calls back into your type, and what happens if it panics and never returns.

Where foreign code runs In the shelf Ask
a closure parameter make in fill_with can it call push or get? can it panic?
an iterator's next or len extend_exact is len a lie? does next change the container?
a destructor clear, Drop if it panics, will something drop this element again?
Clone, Eq, Ord, Hash, Deref, Borrow none can two calls disagree? can one panic half-way?

Keep the fields private. When soundness depends on a field, the whole module that can reach the field is part of the proof. Privacy stops code outside the module from breaking it (Working with unsafe).

This crate denies two lints in Cargo.toml:

Tested here: after deleting the comment in push, cargo clippy fails with unsafe block missing a safety comment. The lint checks that a comment exists, not that it is true. The planted variants carry comments that say SAFETY: WRONG, which is enough for the lint.

05

Attack your own safe API

Write tests as the worst caller safe Rust allows. tests/hostile.rs has a test for each attack. Each planted variant is a plausible "optimisation" of one method, behind a Cargo feature that is off by default.

Safe code may Attack in the test What a sound version does
return any number from len() claim 0 and yield 7; claim usize::MAX uses len only to refuse early, and checks the real bound on every write
change the container from inside an iterator next() pushes to the shelf re-reads len after every call into caller code
call back from a closure push and keep the &T; read everything while filling publishes an element only once it is written, and does not cache len across the call
panic anywhere the closure panics on its third call never lets len cover an unwritten slot
panic in Drop one destructor panics during clear shrinks len before dropping
Watch out

The planted variants execute real UB. The crate refuses to compile them in a normal build: compile_error! fires unless the build is under Miri (cfg(miri)) or you pass --cfg planted_native for a sanitizer run. So plain cargo test and cargo run cannot reach them. One side effect: cargo test --all-features fails to compile, on purpose.

A trait that lies

This takes no unsafe to write:

The planted extend_exact checks len() once, then writes without a bounds check:

The standard library's docs for ExactSizeIterator say the same thing: it is a safe trait, so unsafe code must not rely on its length being correct (docs).

An honest iterator can break this code too. In iterator_that_pushes_while_being_consumed, len() is correct and there is room when it is checked. Then each call to next() pushes to the shelf, and the room is gone. The sound version asks push, which checks the real bound each time:

Re-entrancy

A method that takes &self can be called again while it is already running. The sound fill_with keeps nothing from before the call to make that make could have changed:

The planted stale-index version reads len once, before the loop:

The standard library meets the same hazard in OnceCell: its docs say re-entrant initialisation from the closure is an error and panics. A comment in the implementation says some forms of re-entrant initialisation might lead to UB (once.rs, Rust 1.98.1).

A panic half-way

The planted early-len version reserves the whole range first:

If make panics, the stack unwinds, Drop runs and drops slots that were never written. make can also simply call get and read one. The Rustonomicon calls the minimum requirement here minimal exception safety: unwinding must not break memory safety. Its example is this mistake: set_len first, then a clone that can panic (Exception safety). The standard library's general Vec extend loop raises the length once per element, and its comment says why: next() is user code that can panic (extend_desugared, Rust 1.98.1).

A destructor that panics

The same rule, mirrored. clear shrinks len before it drops, so a panic leaves the shelf claiming only elements it still owns. The test's element panics only on its first drop:

Testing

The "first drop only" detail matters. An element that panics on every drop turns a double drop into a panic during unwinding, which aborts the test process instead of failing one assertion. That happened to an earlier form of this test when the bug was planted.

Also test the shapes that have no bad intent: capacity 0, a zero-sized T and an over-aligned T. One test in tests/hostile.rs covers all three.

06

Miri

Miri is an interpreter that runs your tests and stops at the first undefined behaviour it detects. It needs nightly.

Tested here, sound version: all tests and doctests pass under both aliasing models. Each full run took about 15 to 18 s of wall time on this machine, including cargo's own steps. The test harness's "finished in" line is not wall time under Miri: one test reported 25.68 s inside a run of about 15 s. By default Miri replaces the clock with a deterministic fake one.

The crate scales its random tests down under Miri with cfg!(miri): 4 honest rounds instead of 2,000, and 24 scripts instead of 5,000. Under Miri you search far fewer inputs, so keep the native run too.

Tested here, planted versions (same results under both aliasing models):

Variant Well-behaved model test Hostile tests where Miri reports UB Hostile tests that fail only by assertion Random script test
planted-lying-len passes claims too little; pushes while consumed none stops at std's bounds precondition
planted-stale-index passes pushes and keeps the reference none fails: length differs from model
planted-early-len passes reads while filling; panics half-way pushes and keeps the reference fails: contents differ from model
planted-wrong-get fails by assertion none five of the eight fails: contents differ from model

Read the first three rows again. A well-behaved test suite under Miri says nothing about hostile callers. Miri's README says it directly: it can only tell you whether a particular way of using your code caused UB in a particular execution. A passing run does not show the code is sound.

The last row is the other half: Miri had no complaint about wrong answers. Only the assertions caught them.

Real output: the re-entrant write

Stacked Borrows, trimmed where marked [...]:

Read the two help: blocks first. They give the line that created the reference and the line that invalidated it. The headline error is only where the dead reference was next used.

Tree Borrows reports the same two lines in other words: reborrow through <136033> at alloc44374[0x0] is forbidden, because the tag became Disabled due to a foreign write access. Both messages call the aliasing rules experimental.

Real output: the panic half-way

The backtrace under it runs from Shelf::drop through clear and assume_init_drop into the element's destructor. For reads_the_shelf_while_filling the report also comes from a destructor: the test's own length assertion panics first, and unwinding then drops the unwritten slots.

The lying length: std reports first

For planted-lying-len the first thing to fire is not a Miri diagnostic. It is a debug check inside the standard library.

Both outputshow to reach Miri's own diagnostic

With RUSTFLAGS=-Zub-checks=no that check is off, and Miri reports the UB itself:

Leaks

A variation (a scratch test, not in code/): the re-entrant push without keeping the reference, under planted-stale-index. No dead reference is ever used. The test itself passes, then Miri reports memory leaked: alloc42076 (Rust heap, size: 11, align: 1): the overwritten String was never dropped.

What Miri does not do

These points are from its README:

  • It checks only what runs, with the inputs you give. Addresses and thread schedules are choices too; -Zmiri-many-seeds tries more of them. This crate has no threads, so it was not used here.
  • It supports few foreign functions and platform APIs, so some FFI and I/O code cannot run.
  • Stacked Borrows and Tree Borrows are experimental models. It follows its own approximation of what is UB and makes no promise about future compiler versions.
  • If your code depends on unspecified layout, a run can pass and the code can still break on another compiler or platform.
07

Sanitizers

A sanitizer adds checks to the native program. It runs real system calls and foreign code, and does not interpret. The flags are unstable. The unstable book lists AddressSanitizer (ASan) and ThreadSanitizer for aarch64-apple-darwin; its MemorySanitizer list has no macOS target.

--cfg planted_native unlocks the planted code, so this command does execute UB natively. Run it only on purpose. With an explicit --target, cargo keeps RUSTFLAGS off build scripts and procedural macros.

Tested here, one test per process. Adding -Zbuild-std (which also instruments the standard library) gave the same pass or fail results.

Build Hostile test ASan What failed the test
sound the five iterator and closure tests silent nothing, all pass
lying-len claims too little; pushes while consumed silent: std's debug check fired first the precondition panic
lying-len, -Zub-checks=no the same two stack-buffer-overflow ASan
stale-index pushes and keeps the reference silent only the test's assertion
early-len reads while filling; pushes and keeps the reference silent only the tests' assertions
early-len panics half-way SEGV on unknown address 0x000000000010 a crash inside the destructor

(The -Zub-checks=no run was done without -Zbuild-std.)

ASan saw the write past the end of the stack object. It said nothing about overwriting a slot that a live reference pointed to: that address is valid memory. The SEGV is not a diagnosis of uninitialised memory either. The program followed a bad pointer and crashed.

With ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1, the leak variation from the Miri section also produced LeakSanitizer: detected memory leaks, Direct leak of 11 byte(s), on this Mac.

ThreadSanitizer was not run: Shelf is !Sync, and the crate starts no threads of its own. cargo careful, which rebuilds the standard library with debug assertions and extra checks, was not installed (its README says it works with FFI and is much faster than Miri, but detects less).

In production

Use a sanitizer where Miri cannot go: code that calls C, or workloads too slow to interpret. Instrument the C side too when you can. The unstable book says ASan works with uninstrumented code but detects less.

08

Fuzz the safe wrapper

Do not fuzz one method with one random argument. Fuzz sequences of operations, including hostile caller behaviour. script::run(&[u8]) reads a byte string as a program: which method to call, how much the iterator lies, whether the closure pushes, reads or panics. Any byte string is a valid program.

In code/, tests/script.rs feeds it 5,000 seeded random strings natively and 24 under Miri. This is random testing, not coverage-guided fuzzing. It needs no dependencies and replays from a seed. It also asserts that the hostile paths were reached, so a decoding mistake cannot turn it into a test of nothing:

One trap with injected panics: libfuzzer-sys installs a panic hook that aborts the process (source, read at version 0.4.12). A closure that calls panic! would end the fuzz run, even inside catch_unwind. resume_unwind starts unwinding without calling the hook:

This needs panic = "unwind". With panic = "abort", nothing can be caught.

The cargo-fuzz target would be as follows. It was not compiled or run, because cargo-fuzz is not installed here.

A fuzzer finds only what its oracle notices. Keep the model and ledger in the target. libFuzzer builds can add AddressSanitizer, which has the blind spots shown above. So keep the inputs it finds and replay them under Miri.

For richer inputs, the Rust Fuzz Book describes structure-aware fuzzing, including a data structure compared with a known-good model.

09

Bounded model checking with Kani

Kani treats a proof harness like a test whose inputs are all possible values: kani::any() stands for every value of a type. It checks panics, failed assertions and several kinds of memory error. Kani was not installed or run for this page. This section reports its documentation.

Where it fits: small, loop-bounded cores such as index arithmetic, where "every claimed value" is worth more than thousands of random ones.

Limit, from Kani's docs What it means here
Loops need a bound, and a proof covers only sizes within it (unwinding) a result for capacity 2 and 4 items says nothing certain about 1,000
It does not track reference lifetimes, so it does not detect aliasing violations as such (UB page) the stale-index bug would need an assertion that sees the changed value
Detecting reads of uninitialised memory is partial and experimental (feature support) do not rely on it for early-len by default
It focuses on sequential code (UB page) it does not look for data races

So a successful Kani run is not "no UB". It is "these properties hold for these bounded inputs, for the kinds of error Kani checks".

10

Compile-fail tests

Some of the safety argument is carried by types: "this cannot be shared between threads", "you cannot call clear while holding a reference". Test that the forbidden programs do not compile. Otherwise a later unsafe impl, or a signature changed from &mut self to &self, removes the guarantee and every run-time test still passes.

rustdoc's compile_fail code blocks do this with no extra crate. src/lib.rs has five:

Must not compile Expected error What it protects
require Shelf<u8, 4>: Sync E0277 invariant 4
require Shelf<Rc<u8>, 4>: Send E0277 no Rc crosses threads
clear() while a returned &T is alive E0502 clear's safety comment
move the shelf while a &T is alive E0505 elements are stored inline
view Shelf<&'static str> as Shelf<&'a str> lifetime error with no code invariance

The idea in the first row, reduced to the standard library: a type that holds a Cell is not Sync. This snippet is compiled by the page checker, which requires this error code.

Why invariance is on the list

The last row matters because of push(&self). If Shelf<T> were covariant, safe code could view a shelf of long-lived references as a shelf of short-lived ones, push a short-lived reference, and read it through the original shelf after it died. UnsafeCell<T> makes the type invariant in T. Compiling the same signature against a small UnsafeCell wrapper, rustc reported lifetime may not live long enough and named invariance as the reason.

Two ways to pass for the wrong reason

  1. Any error counts. A misspelt name also fails to compile. Here each is paired with a twin block that differs only by the forbidden step and must compile. The first two share one twin, which asks whether Shelf<u8, 4> is Send.
  2. Stable ignores the error code. Checking the code in compile_fail,E0277 is a nightly feature. Tested here: after changing E0277 to the wrong code E0502, stable cargo test --doc passed all 9 doctests. Nightly failed two with Some expected error codes were not found. Run cargo +nightly test --doc in CI.

For many cases, or to check full compiler messages, look at a crate such as trybuild (not used or reviewed here).

11

Show that each check can fail

A test that has never failed has not been shown to test anything. Break the code and require a specific failure.

Planted soundness bugs. code/check-planted.sh runs four planted variants under Miri. For each it demands a failing run and the expected text. "The command failed" alone is not evidence: a typo also fails. Real output:

With one expected string changed to nonsense in a copy of the script, that line read MISSED and the script exited 1.

One-off mutations, made in a scratch copy with stable (nightly for the Sync one):

Mutation What failed
clear drops before it shrinks len destructor_that_panics_during_clear: a destructor ran twice
Drop does nothing the destructor test, closure_that_panics_half_way, the script ledger
add unsafe impl Sync the Sync compile-fail doctest
remove the early NoRoom refusal iterator_that_claims_too_much, the model test, the script test
remove the "full" check in fill_with the capacity-0 test: make ran with no room
get hides the last element eight tests, including the model, the script and the twin comparison

The invariance doctest has not been mutated this way: making the real type covariant means rewriting its fields.

Tip

After you fix a real soundness bug, keep the hostile test that reproduced it, and confirm once that it fails without the fix under the tool that is meant to catch it.

12

What did the unsafe buy?

Benchmark the unsafe version against the best safe version you can write, not against a careless one. Here that is SafeShelf, built on OnceCell:

examples/bench.rs times two workloads with u64 elements and N = 1024: create a shelf, push N values and sum them through get; and sum an already filled shelf. It takes 31 samples of 2,000 repetitions per case, alternates the cases, and prints median, fastest and slowest.

Measured here: Apple M4 Pro, macOS 27.0, rustc 1.98.1, default release profile, 2026-11-26. Range of the medians over four runs, in ns per element:

Workload Shelf SafeShelf Safe takes
new + fill + sum 0.744 to 0.804 1.110 to 1.185 about 1.5 times as long
sum only 0.347 to 0.369 0.393 to 0.416 about 13% longer

Some single samples were far slower than the median (up to 14.5 ns in one run). That is why the table uses medians. The machine was not isolated: other builds may have been running.

Size is exact, from size_of, and depends on T:

N = 1024 Shelf SafeShelf
u64 8,200 bytes 16,392 bytes
String 24,584 bytes 24,584 bytes

OnceCell<T> has to record whether it is filled. With u64 there is no spare bit pattern for that, so each slot doubles. String has one on this compiler, so the sizes match. This is an observation about this compiler, not a layout guarantee. The benchmark does not time String elements, and the timing differences were not profiled.

How to read it: for u64-like elements on a hot path, the unsafe version has a measured speed and size advantage. If your elements look like String or your path is not hot, this page gives no evidence that the unsafe is worth it, and the safe version is the sensible default: it needs none of the machinery above to rule out memory errors in its own code.

Tip

Report the machine, compiler, profile, element type, size, sample count and spread. Say what you did not measure. A single speed-up factor with none of these cannot be checked.

13

When each check runs in CI

This schedule is advice. Adjust it to your crate's run times.

When Check Command
every pull request native tests, including hostile, script and doctests cargo test
every pull request safety-comment lint cargo clippy --all-targets -- -D warnings
every pull request that can affect the unsafe code Miri, both aliasing models the first two commands in the Miri section
every pull request that can affect it compile-fail error codes cargo +nightly test --doc
nightly AddressSanitizer on the sound build, leak detection on ASAN_OPTIONS=detect_leaks=1 with the command under Sanitizers, without features
nightly or continuous coverage-guided fuzzing for a fixed time; replay the corpus under tests cargo fuzz run (not run here)
nightly the checks still catch the planted bugs ./check-planted.sh
before a release, or when a bounded core changes Kani harnesses cargo kani (not run here)
when there are threads ThreadSanitizer, -Zmiri-many-seeds, a model checker such as loom does not apply to this crate

Pin the nightly version in CI. A new nightly can change what Miri or a sanitizer reports, and you want that to arrive as a deliberate update. Do not let a tool's skip count as a pass: if Miri cannot run a test, mark it #[cfg_attr(miri, ignore)] with a reason, and cover it another way.

In production

Review remains part of the process. These tools check executions, bounded inputs or types. None of the ones used here proves that every safe caller is harmless. The research tool Rudra (now archived) searched for three patterns worth checking by hand: panic safety, assumptions about what safe trait methods return, and wrong Send/Sync bounds on generic types.

Terms
undefined behaviour (UB)An operation the language rules forbid; a program that performs it has no guaranteed meaning.
soundNo use of the API from safe code can cause undefined behaviour.
invariantA fact about the data that unsafe code assumes is true at the points where it relies on it.
oracleThe part of a test that decides whether a behaviour was wrong.
re-entrancyCaller code, run by a method, calls back into the same object before the method has finished.
panic safetyAn unwind from any call leaves data that can be dropped or used without breaking memory safety.

COMPLETE PROJECTS · BUILD

A mini key-value store: log, memtable, sorted tables

A small embedded key-value store in the style of a log-structured merge (LSM) tree: write-ahead log, sorted memtable, immutable table files with bloom filters, and full compaction. It is a readable model of the idea, not a database to ship.

9sections
1216lines you can run
22tests passed, recorded
Draftnot reviewed by you
Where it sits
  1. Callers
  2. Store: put, get, delete, scan
  3. Memtable and write-ahead log
  4. SSTables, bloom filters, compaction
  5. File system
IN 60 SECONDS
  • A write is appended to a write-ahead log (WAL) and then placed in a sorted map in memory, the memtable.
  • When enough has been written, the memtable becomes an immutable sorted file (an SSTable); deletes are stored as tombstones.
  • A read checks the memtable, then tables from newest to oldest, and stops at the first answer, even a tombstone.
  • Compaction merges all tables into one; it must delete the old files oldest first, or a crash can bring deleted keys back.
  • Tested here: acknowledged writes survive killing the process. By design they are not protected against power loss, because the log is never synced.
  • The code has real limits, among them a zero-filled log tail that stops it from opening; each limit listed as tested has a test.
01

What you get, and what it costs

Use it to see how an LSM-style engine fits together in code you can read in one sitting, and as a base for experiments. Do not use it to hold data you care about: see the Known limits section.

The idea: never update a file in place. Append each change to a log, collect changes in sorted order in memory, and now and then write them out as a new sorted file. Writing is simple and sequential. The price is paid elsewhere:

Cost In this code
a read may visit many files get walks the tables from newest to oldest
old versions use disk space until you call compact()
compaction rewrites live data again every call rewrites all of it
recovery work open reads every table in full and replays the log

Nothing compacts automatically. A caller that never calls compact collects one table per flush.

The public surface is small. Store has open, put, delete, get, scan, flush and compact. The crate also exports the codec, the bloom filter, the merge and read access to tables, so that tests can check them.

cargo run in the lab walks through writes, flushes, a reopen and a compaction, and prints the files after each step.

02

The parts

File in code/src/ Job
store.rs open (which is also recovery), put, delete, get, scan, flush, compact
wal.rs frames, replay, truncation of a torn tail
sstable.rs writing and reading one immutable table
bloom.rs "definitely not in this table"
merge.rs k-way merge of sorted runs
codec.rs errors, CRC-32, the record layout, bounds-checked decoding

A directory holds at most one live log, wal.log, and any number of tables, sst_000001.sst and up. A higher number means newer data. There is no separate list of live files: the directory listing is the list.

get follows the same age order:

scan(from, to) returns the keys in [from, to). It reads every record of every table, lays them into a temporary map from oldest to newest, then lays the memtable on top. This is short and clearly correct, but its cost grows with all the data, not with the size of the range. A real engine merges iterators that seek to from.

03

Decisions and trade-offs

Decision Why What it costs
log before memtable a failed append leaves the memtable unchanged, so reads do not show a write the log never accepted every write pays for a log append
no sync of the log a write does not wait for the storage device acknowledged writes can be lost on power failure
a delete is a tombstone (None) older tables may still hold the key deleted keys use space until compaction
BTreeMap memtable ordered iteration for flush and range reads no concurrent writers
one record layout for log and tables one encoder and one decoder to test no prefix compression
sparse index, one key in 16 less memory than indexing every key a lookup reads and decodes a run of up to 16 records
one bloom filter per table lets get skip most tables that lack the key memory per table; no help for scan
compaction merges everything tombstones can always be dropped rewrites all data and holds it all in memory
temp file, sync, rename no half-written table under a final name one device sync per table

The flush threshold counts writes, not live bytes

mem_bytes grows on every insert, including an overwrite of a key already present.

As a measure of memory it overestimates. As a bound on the log it works: every logged write is counted, so rewriting one key cannot grow the log forever. overwriting_one_key_still_triggers_flushes tests this: 500 writes to one key with a threshold of 1,000 make more than 10 tables, and the log stays under 1,500 bytes. If you change the counter to track live bytes, you need a second trigger for log size.

The table file

Byte layout of an SSTabledata, index, bloom, footer

All integers are little-endian.

Part Contents
data records in key order: [tag u8][klen u32][key][vlen u32][value]; tag 0 is a tombstone
index count u32, then for records 0, 16, 32 and so on: [klen u32][key][offset u64]
bloom [k u8][length u32][bits]
footer, 32 bytes data_end u64, bloom_off u64, record_count u64, crc32 u32, magic u32

The CRC covers everything before it. open reads the whole file, checks it, and keeps only the index and the filter. The record count is read and then ignored. The magic number is the only version marker.

To look a key up, get finds the last index entry that is not greater than the key, reads from there to the next entry, and stops early when it passes the key:

Each such lookup opens the file again. There is no block cache and no handle cache.

In Rust

Bytes from disk are untrusted input. The decoders go through take, which uses checked_add and slice::get, so a cut record is an Err, not a panic (record_layout cuts one at every length). One path is not guarded: read_range computes end - start from index offsets that open does not check against each other. A hand-made file with a valid checksum and bad offsets could make it panic or ask for a huge buffer. This is from reading the code; no test builds such a file.

The bloom filter

A bloom filter is a bit array. Adding a key sets k bits; a lookup asks whether all of them are set. "No" is certain. "Yes" can be wrong.

Sizing, hashing and the measured error rate10 bits per key, 4 probes

With m bits, n keys, k probes and ideal hash functions, the usual estimate of the false-positive rate is

p \approx \left(1 - e^{-kn/m}\right)^{k}

For m/n = 10 and k = 4 that is about 1.18% (Bloom filter). The same estimate gives about 0.82% for k = 7, near the optimum (m/n) ln 2. So 4 probes accept some more false positives in exchange for fewer bit tests.

Measured here, deterministic inputs:

Test False positives
one filter of 10,000 keys, 100,000 absent keys (tests/format.rs) 1,210 = 1.21%
the many small tables of the model test (tests/model.rs) 2,980 of 126,600 = about 2.35%

The second rate is about double the first. Why was not investigated, so do not read the 1.18% estimate as a promise for small tables.

The k probe positions come from one 64-bit FNV-1a hash by double hashing:

Watch out

The hash is part of the file format. Filters are stored on disk, so a different hash would test different bits in old files and report false negatives: keys that exist would be skipped. The file has no field for a hash version.

04

Invariants

Invariant Kept by Test that fails when it was broken here
tables are ordered oldest to newest by number sorting in open, next_id model test, compaction crash tests (order reversed in open)
the first record found for a key, newest first, is the answer, even a tombstone get model test, compaction crash tests
a delete writes a tombstone to the log apply cut-log, bit-flip and model tests, and others
until a table is complete and renamed, the log still holds its writes order inside flush a_flush_that_fails_leaves_the_log_intact
after recovery, new log frames follow the last valid frame set_len in Wal::open log_cut_at_every_byte_..., model test
a merge drops tombstones only when asked, and compact asks because it covers every table merge_sources, compact the merge test (flag ignored)
during compaction, old files are deleted oldest first the loop in compact_removing both compaction crash tests

The merge takes its sources newest first. In a min-heap ordered by (key, source number), the newest copy of a key comes out first, and the loop discards the rest:

Passing true for drop_tombstones is safe only because compact merges every table. If you add partial or levelled compaction, a tombstone must survive while any older data outside the merge might hold its key. LevelDB drops deletion markers only when no higher-numbered level has a file whose range overlaps the key (impl.md).

05

Compaction: the order of deletes matters

The new table holds no tombstones. While old files are being deleted, the directory holds the new table and some old ones. Reads then depend on which old ones are left.

Deleting oldest first, the old files left behind are always the newest ones. If an old value of a is still there, every newer version or tombstone of a is still there too, and shadows it.

The comment in the original single-file example explains crash safety by saying that the new table shadows the old data. That is not enough for a deleted key, which the new table does not contain. The code is correct because of the delete order, which that comment does not mention.

How this is tested. The original has no test that stops a compaction half-way. For this page, the delete loop takes a limit, and crash_during_compaction(n) stops after n removals. It consumes the store, so a test must reopen the directory. compact() passes no effective limit and behaves as before.

Tested here: with .rev() added to the delete loop, both compaction crash tests fail.

This argument assumes that the file system keeps the removals in the order they were made. That holds for what a running system sees after a process dies. After power loss it is not established: this code never syncs the directory.

06

Crash and recovery: what is true

Two different failures are often both called "a crash". In a process crash the program dies and the operating system keeps running: data already passed to write is still in the kernel, which holds it for the next reader. In a power loss or OS crash, data that had not reached storage can vanish.

Event What the code does Evidence
process killed at any moment every acknowledged write is there after reopen tested with SIGKILL, 12 kill points per run
last log record cut short that record is dropped and cut off the file tested at every byte of a sample log
one bit flipped in the log replay keeps the records before it and discards the rest, silently tested for every bit of a sample log
temp file left over removed at open tested
new table in place, log not yet reset replay repeats writes already in the table; reads are unchanged tested by rebuilding that disk state
compaction stopped between deletes contents unchanged tested after each number of deletes
a table file changed before open open fails with Corrupt tested: every byte inverted, every shorter length
power loss or OS crash no guarantee not testable here; reasoned below

Replay

Replay stops at the first frame that is short or fails its checksum. Wal::open then truncates the file there, so later appends never land behind bad bytes. A frame with a good checksum but a bad record is different: that is not a torn write, so open returns an error.

The weak point: replay cannot tell a torn last write from damage in the middle. Both end replay, and truncation then destroys every later record, with no error and no count. RocksDB makes this a setting. Its default, kPointInTimeRecovery, also stops replay at the first inconsistency, while kAbsoluteConsistency expects no corruption at all (options.h). LevelDB's log is cut into 32 KB blocks so that a reader can resynchronise after corruption (log format). Here the CRC also leaves the length field uncovered.

Killing a real process

The model test's "crash" is drop(store). That is a useful reopen test, but destructors still run. So tests/recovery.rs also starts the test binary again as a child. The child writes keys, compacts every 90 operations, and prints ack i only after the call for operation i has returned. The parent reads acknowledgements, sends SIGKILL, checks that the child really died of signal 9, and reopens.

The assertion allows for timing: the recovered contents must equal the state after the first n operations, for some n that includes every acknowledged one. It passed 15 runs in a row here, after a first version of the test was fixed: that version closed the pipe before the kill, so the child could die of a write error instead.

The test does not record which step each kill interrupted. It cannot be relied on to hit a particular window; the tests that build one state each are there for that. In the mutation runs below it failed for several planted bugs, among them a user-space buffer (BufWriter) around the log and a log reset before the table write.

Power loss

This part is reasoning from the code and documentation. No power-loss test was run.

  • Wal::append calls write_all and never sync_data. An acknowledged write may be only in the kernel's cache.
  • SsTable::write syncs the file's contents, then renames. It does not sync the directory. Linux's fsync(2) says that syncing a file does not necessarily make its directory entry durable, and that the directory needs its own sync. The safe recipe is write, sync the file, rename, sync the directory (LWN).
  • So after flush or compact, the later steps (resetting the log, removing old tables) could become durable while the rename did not. That would lose data that had already been synced inside the new table.
In Rust

sync_all and sync_data are not the same system call on every platform. In the Rust 1.98.1 standard library, on Apple targets both call fcntl(F_FULLFSYNC) (read in std/src/sys/fs/unix.rs). On Linux, measure and reason about fsync and fdatasync separately.

In production

To claim durability, choose when a write is acknowledged: after its own sync, or after a shared one (group commit). Sync the directory after creating or renaming files, and before deleting what they replace. Then test with a tool that can drop unsynced writes. None of this is in the code, and these changes were not tried.

07

Known limits

tests/limitations.rs pins the first seven rows. Each of those tests passes because the limit is real, so a fix makes it fail, and you replace it with a test of the new behaviour.

Limit Consequence Test
eight zero bytes at the log tail parse as a frame of length 0 with a matching CRC open returns Corrupt: the store will not start a_zero_filled_log_tail_stops_...
bytes from a partial append stay in the file later writes return Ok but disappear at the next open bytes_left_by_a_partial_append_... (junk added by hand)
a flush can fail after the write was applied put returns Err, yet the value is readable and survives reopen an_error_from_put_does_not_mean_...
tables are checked only at open damage after that is returned as a normal value a_table_damaged_after_open_...
scan with from > to panics if the memtable has entries; returns empty if it is empty scan_with_reversed_bounds_panics_...
no lock on the directory two Store values overwrite each other's tables two_stores_on_one_directory_lose_data
the threshold counts writes overwrites cause flushes (intended, see above) overwriting_one_key_still_triggers_flushes
lengths are cast to u32 a key, value or frame of 4 GiB or more would be written wrongly none; from the code
.tmp files are removed on open any file with that ending in the directory is deleted partly: the leftover-table test

The zero tail

The CRC-32 of an empty input is 0. A header of eight zero bytes therefore passes the checksum, and decoding an empty record fails. LevelDB's log reader has an explicit case for records of type zero and length zero, which it skips because its memory-mapped writer preallocates file regions (log_reader.cc). RocksDB's comments also mention tolerating zeroed bytes left by preallocation. This store does not preallocate. Whether a crash on your file system can leave zeros after the last record was not tested; if it does, this code does not recover by itself. One possible fix is to treat len == 0 as the end of the log, since a real record is at least 9 bytes.

The scan panic

scan passes its bounds to BTreeMap::range, which documents a panic when the start is greater than the end. The empty-memtable case does not panic because the standard library never searches a map with no root. That is an implementation detail, not a promise.

08

How it is tested

Suite Idea Oracle
model.rs 3 seeds of 7,000 random operations: put, delete, get, scan, flush, compact, reopen, torn tail a BTreeMap
recovery.rs one disk state or event per test, and the process kill the model after a known number of operations
format.rs CRC check value, record bytes, merge rule, corruption of a table, bloom error rate fixed expected values
limitations.rs what does not work the limit itself

The model test also asserts that it reached what it claims to cover. With these seeds it runs 832 reopen "crashes", 337 torn tails, 654 explicit flushes and 430 compaction calls, with up to 15 tables. The original single-file example, run here with the same seeds, printed the same tally, including the same 2,980 bloom false positives in 126,600 probes. That is good evidence that the split kept the behaviour; it is not a proof.

The strongest tests are exhaustive over a small space. This one cuts the log at every byte, and then writes again after recovery to show that nothing was left in the way:

Can these tests fail?

Each change below was made alone in a scratch copy, then cargo test --release was run.

Planted bug Tests that failed
delete old tables newest first 2: both compaction crash tests
reset the log before writing the table 3: failed flush, put error, process kill
do not truncate the torn tail 2: cut-log, model
skip the log checksum (except for empty frames) 2: bit flip, partial append
weaken the table checksum check 1: every-byte corruption
get searches the oldest table first 3: both compaction crash tests, model
compaction treats the oldest table as newest 4: both compaction crash tests, process kill, model
keep leftover temp files 1: leftover temp file
do not log deletes 5, including cut-log and model
buffer the log in user space 4: cut-log, bit flip, process kill, partial append
reverse the table order in open 4: both compaction crash tests, process kill, model
the merge drops tombstones even when told not to 1: the merge test
remove sync_all before the rename none

Note the sync_all row. No test here can see a missing sync, because a running operating system shows unsynced data to the next reader. Failures of the process-kill test can depend on timing. In this run, every bug it caught was also caught by another test.

This exercise also found a weak test. With the user-space buffer, the cut-log and bit-flip tests first passed: they read the log file while it was still empty, so their loops had nothing to check. They now assert that the file holds the whole log.

Also not tested: a failing write, rename or remove_file other than through the blocked temp path; a full disk; power loss; a second process; very large keys and values.

Testing

To make a file operation fail on purpose without a mocking layer, one cheap trick works here: create a directory where the code wants to create its temp file. It makes the table write fail at a known point. It covers only that one point.

09

Where to take it

These are suggestions in a sensible order, not tested here.

  1. Fix the recovery limits: the zero tail, an append that fails part-way (cut the log back to the last good length, or refuse further writes), and a clear result for put when only the flush failed.
  2. Say what durable means: sync policy for the log, and directory syncs around rename and delete.
  3. Lock the directory, so a second writer is refused.
  4. Checksum blocks and verify on every read, so late damage is detected.
  5. Stream the merge, so that compaction and scan do not load whole tables.
  6. Compact in levels. LevelDB keeps a young level plus levels with non-overlapping files and a size limit for each, and records the live files in a manifest (impl.md). With partial compaction, both the tombstone rule and the delete-order argument above have to be redone.
  7. Then add concurrency: immutable memtables flushed in the background, and readers that hold a consistent set of tables.

To build a fuller engine step by step, see the mini-lsm course.

LSM treeA storage design that buffers writes in memory, writes them out as sorted immutable files, and merges those files later.
memtableThe sorted in-memory table that holds the newest writes.
SSTableA sorted string table: an immutable file of records in key order.
tombstoneA stored record that says a key was deleted.
compactionMerging tables to drop old versions and, when safe, tombstones.
write-ahead log (WAL)A file that receives each change before the change is applied to the in-memory state.
torn writeA write of which only a part is present after a failure.
